original_question: Let X be a non-empty class of finite groups of odd order closed under taking subgroups, homomorphic images, and extensions. Let H be an X-maximal subgroup of a finite group G, and N a normal subgroup of G. Must H ∩ N be an X-maximal subgroup of N?
target_in_paper: Problem 21.57 in the section "New Problems (21st issue, 2026)" of The Kourovka Notebook.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the paper's target almost verbatim: it has the correct closure hypotheses on X, the odd-order restriction on the groups in X, the ambient data of a finite group G with a normal subgroup N, an X-maximal subgroup H of G, and the exact question whether H ∩ N must be X-maximal in N.
missing_details: For a fully stand-alone formulation, the term "X-maximal subgroup" should be defined explicitly: H <= G, H belongs to X, and whenever H <= K <= G with K in X, one has K = H.

The universal quantification should be made explicit: the question asks whether this conclusion must hold for every nonempty class X with the stated properties and for every finite group G, normal subgroup N of G, and X-maximal subgroup H of G.
It helps to state explicitly that every group belonging to X is finite and has odd order.
refined_question: Let X be a nonempty class of finite groups such that every group in X has odd order and X is closed under taking subgroups, homomorphic images, and extensions. Suppose G is a finite group, N is a normal subgroup of G, and H <= G is X-maximal, meaning that H belongs to X and no subgroup K with H < K <= G belongs to X. Must H ∩ N be an X-maximal subgroup of N?
justification: In arXiv:1401.0300 as currently posted, your draft matches Problem 21.57 essentially word for word. There is no narrower neighboring conjecture or theorem in this paper that more faithfully represents the intended question, so the official problem statement itself is the right target. Because the notebook problem is extremely concise, the only substantive refinement needed is to unpack the standard term "X-maximal subgroup" and to make the universal quantifiers explicit. No additional ambient hypotheses, degree conditions, field assumptions, or asymptotic qualifiers occur here.
